summary: A Network Host Status report covering April 24 to May 5, 1972. The USC IBM 360/44 became a network user during that time. It updates RFC 332. It was replaced by RFC 344.

eli5.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

subtitle: Checking which network hosts were working in late April and early May 1972

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed current information about which hosts were functioning as network servers.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested network hosts daily from April 24 to May 5, 1972, reporting whether each host was dead, open, half-open, timed out, refused, or full (unable to accept new connections).
tldr.outcome: This periodic status report allowed users to locate available network services. The USC IBM 360/44 became a new network user during this period.

today: RFC 344 replaced this status report later in May 1972. These periodic reports tracked ARPANET growth during its formative period.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 342 reports on host status from April 24 to May 5, 1972. During this interval, the IBM 360/44 at USC (Network Address 23) became a new network user, expanding the operational ARPANET. BBN conducted daily tests from the Terminal IMP to determine each host's accessibility and responsiveness.
sections.eli5: BBN kept checking which big computers connected to the ARPANET were working. More computers were joining the network during this time.

sections.title: Host Categories and Status Codes
sections.content:
Like previous reports, hosts were divided into two categories for testing: non-server hosts (such as MIT-AI and Case, expected to join later) and user-only hosts including Terminal IMPs and machines at Rand, Harvard, Illinois, NBS, and USC. The 1972 network also introduced a new status code: F (Full), indicating a host opened a connection but reported all network ports in use.

The full set of codes used were: O (Open), D (Dead), H (Half Open), T (Timed out), R (Refused), and F (Full). The testing revealed varying reliability across the network, with some machines like SRI-AI remaining consistently dead throughout the period.
sections.eli5: Some computers only received data (user-only), while others let other sites use them. The new F code meant a computer was so busy it wouldn't accept more connections. Different computers had different reliability.

sections.title: Network Growth
sections.content:
The status tables across this period show a maturing network. Major servers like UCLA, SRI, UCSB, UTAH, MIT-Multics, RAND CSG, SDC, Harvard, and Carnegie were becoming more consistently available. The addition of USC and the expected addition of MIT-AI and Stanford (which had not yet become servers) showed the network expanding to new institutions.

Performance issues persisted: AMES-67 remained dead throughout, and other hosts showed intermittent problems. Despite these issues, the network was stabilizing into a core of reliable servers that researchers could depend on.
sections.eli5: More places were joining and sharing computers. Some computers were very reliable, but some were always down or often had problems. The network was growing and getting better over time.
